hello.title: Hello, Pascal!
hello.summary: Write your first Pascal program and print text and numbers with writeln and write.
hello.lesson.0: A Pascal program starts with the word `program` and a name. The code that runs goes between `begin` and `end.` (with a period). The program runs these lines from top to bottom.
hello.lesson.2: Line by line: `program Hello;` gives the program a name. `{$mode objfpc}{$H+}` is a **compiler directive**: it tells Free Pascal to use its modern mode and long strings. Every program in this course has this line. `begin` and `end.` mark the main block, and `writeln` prints a line.
hello.lesson.4: Text goes in single quotes, like `'Hello'`. Such a text is called a **string**. `writeln` can print several values separated by commas. It prints them one after the other without spaces and then ends the line. `writeln` alone prints an empty line.
hello.lesson.6: `write` prints like `writeln`, but it does not end the line. The next output continues on the same line. A semicolon `;` separates two statements. Before `end` you may leave it out.
hello.lesson.9: Numbers do not need quotes. Without quotes, Pascal calculates: `2 + 3` gives `5`, but `'2 + 3'` is only text. Use `*` to multiply. You can mix text and numbers in one `writeln`.
hello.lesson.11: Pascal does not care about upper and lower case in names: `writeln`, `WriteLn` and `WRITELN` are the same. Text between `{` and `}` or after `//` is a **comment**, and the compiler ignores it. A `{` followed by `$` is a directive, not a comment.
hello.lesson.12: Strings use single quotes, never double quotes. To put an apostrophe inside a string, write it twice: `'It''s late'` prints `It's late`. The last `end` of the program needs a period, not a semicolon.
hello.card.1: `{$mode objfpc}{$H+}` turns on modern Free Pascal
hello.card.2: `writeln('Hi')` prints and ends the line, `write` stays on it
hello.card.3: `writeln('Sum: ', 2 + 3)` prints values one after the other
hello.card.4: `'It''s'`: write an apostrophe twice inside a string

variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Declare variables with var, store values with := and use integer, real, char, string, boolean and const.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** is a name for a value that the program stores. In Pascal you declare every variable before `begin`, in a `var` section: the name, a colon `:` and the **type**. Then `:=` stores a value in it. Read `x := 5` as "x becomes 5".
variables.lesson.2: `age := age + 1` takes the old value of `age`, adds 1 and stores the result in `age` again. A single `=` does not store anything: it compares two values. You use it in conditions later.
variables.lesson.4: The most common types: `integer` holds whole numbers, `real` holds numbers with decimals, `char` holds one character in single quotes, `string` holds text and `boolean` holds `True` or `False`. You can declare several variables of the same type in one line, separated by commas.
variables.lesson.6: `writeln` shows a `real` in scientific notation with a space in front: `2.5000000000000000E+000` means 2.5 times 10 to the power of 0. The next unit shows how to print it as `2.50`. A `boolean` is printed in capital letters: `TRUE` or `FALSE`.
variables.lesson.8: A **constant** is a value that never changes. You declare it in a `const` section with `=` (not `:=`) and without a type: Pascal sees the type from the value. Constants make code easier to read and to change.
variables.lesson.10: The operator `+` joins two strings into a new, longer string.
variables.lesson.12: Pascal checks types. `count := 2.5` is an error when `count` is an `integer`, because an integer cannot hold decimals. The other way round works: `price := 3` stores `3.0` in a `real`. Always give a variable a value before you read it.
variables.lesson.13: Names start with a letter or `_` and may contain letters, digits and `_`. Upper and lower case do not matter: `Total` and `total` are the same name. That is why a variable must not have the same name as the program.
variables.card.0: `var x: integer;` declares a variable before `begin`
variables.card.3: `const Max = 10;` is a value that never changes
variables-1.prompt: Which line stores 10 in the variable `x`?

variables-3.explain: `+` joins the strings in the order you write them: first `b`, then `a`.

variables-4.explain: A constant never changes. Trying to assign a new value is a compile error.

variables-12.explain: Strings use single quotes in Pascal. Write `city := 'Rome';`.
operators.title: Operators and formatting
operators.summary: Calculate with + - * /, divide whole numbers with div and mod, and format output with :width:decimals.
operators.lesson.0: `+`, `-` and `*` work with integers and reals. The operator `/` always gives a `real`, even for two integers. To divide whole numbers, use `div`: it gives the result without the remainder. `mod` gives the remainder.
operators.lesson.2: `mod` is useful to test numbers: `n mod 2` is `0` for even numbers. `*`, `/`, `div` and `mod` are calculated before `+` and `-`. Use parentheses `(` `)` to change the order.
operators.lesson.5: In `writeln`, `value:width` prints the value right-aligned in `width` characters. For a `real`, `value:width:decimals` also sets the number of decimals. A width of `0` means "as wide as needed", so `x:0:2` prints `x` with two decimals.
operators.lesson.7: `round(x)` rounds a real to the nearest whole number. `trunc(x)` cuts off the decimals. Both give an `integer`.
operators.lesson.10: `inc(n)` adds 1 to the variable `n`, and `dec(n)` subtracts 1. With a second value, `inc(n, 5)` adds 5. They are short forms of `n := n + 1` and `n := n - 1`.
operators.lesson.12: You cannot store the result of `/` in an `integer`, even if the division has no remainder: `n := 10 / 2` is a compile error. Use `n := 10 div 2` instead.
operators-1.explain: 4 fits into 23 five times (20). `div` drops the remainder.
operators-3.explain: `div` and `*` come first, from left to right: `6 div 2` is 3, times 3 is 9. Then 2 + 9 = 11.
operators-4.explain: `/` gives a real, and `:0:1` prints it with one decimal.
operators-5.statement: `n := 10 / 2;` works when `n` is an `integer`, because 10 / 2 is 5.
operators-5.explain: `/` always gives a `real`, and a real cannot be stored in an integer. Use `div`.

operators-6.explain: `:0:2` means: as wide as needed, with two decimals.
operators-7.prompt: Complete the line so `rest` gets the remainder 2.
operators-7.explain: `mod` gives the remainder of a whole-number division: 17 = 3 × 5 + 2.

conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Let the program decide with if, then and else, combine conditions with and, or and not, and pick cases with case.
conditions.lesson.0: `if condition then statement` runs the statement only when the condition is true. You compare values with `=` (equal), `<>` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` (less or equal) and `>=` (greater or equal).
conditions.lesson.2: `else` gives a second way: its statement runs when the condition is false. `then` and `else` control only one statement. To run several, put them between `begin` and `end`.
conditions.lesson.4: Never put a semicolon directly before `else`. The semicolon ends the whole `if` statement, so the compiler finds an `else` without an `if`. Write `writeln('Adult')` without `;` when `else` follows.
conditions.lesson.5: To check more than two cases, write `else if`. Pascal tests the conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first branch whose condition is true.
conditions.lesson.8: `and` is true when both sides are true. `or` is true when at least one side is true. `not` turns true into false and false into true. In Pascal, `and` and `or` are calculated before comparisons, so put every comparison in parentheses: `(age >= 18) and (age < 65)`.
conditions.lesson.11: `case value of` picks one branch by value. A label can be one value, a list like `'B', 'C'` or a range like `'D'..'F'`. The `else` branch runs when no label fits. The whole `case` ends with `end;`.
conditions.lesson.13: `case` works with whole numbers and characters, but not with `real` values. It is often easier to read than a long chain of `else if`.

loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with for to/downto do, while do and repeat until, and control loops with break and continue.
loops.lesson.0: A `for` loop repeats a statement a fixed number of times. In `for i := 1 to 3 do`, the **counter** `i` takes the values 1, 2 and 3, one after the other. The counter is a normal variable, so you declare it in the `var` section.
loops.lesson.2: `downto` counts down instead of up. To repeat several statements, put them between `begin` and `end`.
loops.lesson.4: When the start value is already bigger than the end value, a `to` loop does not run at all: `for i := 5 to 1 do` runs zero times. You must not change the counter inside the loop. The compiler does not allow it.
loops.lesson.6: `while condition do` checks the condition before every round. The loop runs as long as the condition is true. If it is false at the start, the loop does not run at all.
loops.lesson.9: `repeat ... until condition` runs its statements first and checks the condition after each round. It stops as soon as the condition is true, so it always runs at least once. Between `repeat` and `until` you need no `begin` and `end`.
loops.lesson.11: `break` leaves the loop at once. `continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes on with the next one.
loops.lesson.13: A `while` or `repeat` loop must change something in its condition. Otherwise it never stops. Remember the difference: `while` goes on while the condition is true, `repeat` stops when the condition is true.
loops.card.0: `for i := 1 to 5 do ...` counts up, `downto` counts down
loops.card.1: `while x > 0 do begin ... end;` checks first
loops.card.2: `repeat ... until x > 10;` runs at least once
loops.card.3: `break` leaves the loop, `continue` skips to the next round

procedures.title: Procedures and functions
procedures.summary: Group code in procedures and functions, pass parameters, return values with Result and change variables with var.
procedures.lesson.0: A **procedure** is a named group of statements. You write it before the main `begin` of the program. Then you **call** it by its name, as often as you like.
procedures.lesson.2: **Parameters** pass values into a procedure. You list them in parentheses with their types and separate groups with `;`. A procedure can have its own `var` section: these **local** variables exist only inside it.
procedures.lesson.5: A **function** calculates a value and gives it back. Its type comes after the parameters, after a colon. Inside, you store the value to give back in `Result`. You use a function call like a value: in `writeln`, in a calculation or in another call.
procedures.lesson.7: `Result` works in the `objfpc` mode of this course. Older Pascal code assigns to the function name instead, like `Square := n * n`. Both give the value back.
procedures.lesson.9: A normal parameter is a **copy**: when the procedure changes it, the variable of the caller stays the same. Write `var` before a parameter to let the procedure work on the caller's variable itself.
procedures.lesson.11: With `var` parameters, a procedure can change several variables. `Swap` exchanges the values of two variables.
procedures.lesson.13: A `var` parameter needs a variable: `AddTen(5)` is a compile error, because `5` is not a variable that can change. Declare a procedure or function before the code that calls it.
procedures.card.2: `var` before a parameter changes the caller's variable

procedures-3.explain: `n` is a copy. Setting the copy to 0 does not change `a`.
procedures-4.statement: In this course's mode, a function gives back its value when you assign it to `Result`.
procedures-4.explain: In `objfpc` mode every function has the variable `Result`. Its value at the end is the return value.

arrays.title: Arrays and strings
arrays.summary: Store many values in arrays, read single characters of a string and use Length, Copy, Pos and UpperCase.
arrays.lesson.0: An **array** stores several values of the same type under one name. `array[1..4] of integer` holds four integers with the **indexes** 1 to 4. You read or change one element with its index in square brackets: `scores[2]`.
arrays.lesson.2: You can give an array its values in the declaration, in parentheses. `Low(a)` gives the first index, `High(a)` the last index and `Length(a)` the number of elements. With them, a loop always fits the array.
arrays.lesson.4: Use only indexes inside the range. For `scores[5]` the compiler warns you, but with a variable index the program may read or change memory that does not belong to the array.
arrays.lesson.6: A string is a row of characters. `s[1]` is the first character, because string indexes start at 1. `Length(s)` gives the number of characters, so `s[Length(s)]` is the last one.
arrays.lesson.9: `Copy(s, start, count)` gives `count` characters from position `start`. `Pos(part, s)` gives the position of `part` in `s`, or `0` if it is not there. `UpperCase` and `LowerCase` change the case, and `IntToStr` turns a number into a string. These three are in the unit `SysUtils`, which you load with `uses SysUtils;` before the `var` section.
arrays.lesson.11: You compare strings with `=` and `<>`. Case matters: `'abc' = 'ABC'` is false. Compare `UpperCase(a) = UpperCase(b)` to ignore case.

arrays.card.2: `s[1]` is the first character of a string

records.title: Records, enumerations and sets
records.summary: Group values in records, name your own values with enumerated types and test membership with sets.
records.lesson.0: A **record** groups several values, called **fields**, under one name. The fields can have different types. You define a new type in a `type` section and end the record with `end;`. A dot gives you one field: `pet.name`.
records.lesson.2: By convention, type names start with `T`. Assigning one record to another copies all fields, so the two variables stay independent. You can also make an array of records.
records.lesson.5: An **enumerated type** lists all its possible values by name: `TSize = (Small, Medium, Large)`. `ord` gives the position of a value, starting at 0. `succ` gives the next value and `pred` the previous one. `writeln` prints the name of the value.
records.lesson.7: Enumerated values work well in `case`. The names make the code easy to read.
records.lesson.10: A **set** holds values of an enumerated type, characters or small numbers. Each value is in the set or not, and there is no order. You write a set in square brackets, like `[Sat, Sun]` or `['a'..'z']`. `x in s` tests if `x` is in the set. `Include(s, x)` adds a value and `Exclude(s, x)` removes it. `+` joins two sets.
records.lesson.12: A set of characters makes a long condition short: `c in ['0'..'9']` is clearer than `(c >= '0') and (c <= '9')`. This program counts the vowels in a word.

records.card.3: `x in [1, 3, 5]` tests if a value is in a set
